p.t: In short
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Know your **break-even** (the sales level where you earn back exactly what you spend) and your target cost per sale before you spend on ads.
Keep **ROAS** (sales money back for each dollar of ads) at **10x** or higher for Google Shopping, or you lose money.

Products under **$200** are usually too cheap to run Google Shopping ads on profitably.
Start small, at **$5 to $30 per day**, and give Google 2 to 4 weeks to learn.
Only advertise products whose **margin** (money you keep per sale) covers the ads, and whose brand enforces **MAP** (the lowest price sellers may advertise).
Why the numbers come before the spend
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Starting ads without knowing your target cost per sale usually leads to overspending.
It also means you take home less profit than planned. **Calculate** the break-even and target CPA before the campaign spends money.

Break-even is the point where sales pay back exactly what you spend, with no profit and no loss. Target CPA (cost per acquisition, here the cost of one sale) is the most you can pay in ads for one sale.
The data you need before scaling paid traffic is the **break-even and target cost per sale**, per product or product group. Scaling means spending more on what works.
Paid traffic means visitors you pay for with ads. Without these answers, you cannot tell when a channel can take more budget or when it must be reduced.

** Compare the actual CPA, ROAS and CPC of running campaigns with the break-even and target figures. CPC is the cost of one click. The gap shows whether to **scale up** a paid channel, keep it, or pull it back.

** Bid and budget changes must be checked against the target cost per sale and target ROAS calculated beforehand. A bid is the price you pay for one click. Without these targets, bid changes are guesses.**
**Guessing with ad money usually loses money.**
** Before raising bids or spend, **check** that the new bid is still profitable at the conversion rate you are actually getting. Conversion rate is the share of visitors who buy.**
**Assuming that more traffic will convert at the same or a better rate is risky and rarely holds.**
** Most sales in this model come from direct-response Google Ads. These are ads that send shoppers straight to a product page.**
**Each product's ad spend must stay profitable after shipping cost and merchant fees (payment fees charged by the payment company), or the sale should not be advertised in that region.**
When starting Google Ads campaigns, the main goal is to **buy data**. Find which search terms (words people type into Google) and products reach your target 1% conversion rate before scaling budget.
In an ideal case, each keyword gets at least **100 clicks** and each product gets at least 100 visitors before you make scaling decisions. A keyword is a search word that triggers your ad.
Break-Even ROAS and target cost per sale
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Run Google Ads at **at or above your break-even ROAS** to avoid losses.
ROAS (return on ad spend) is the sales money you get back for each dollar spent on ads. Below break-even ROAS, you lose money on ads even when sales happen.
Running above break-even creates profit to reinvest or keep.
Use the break-even ROAS as the reference for setting Google Ads bids. ROAS is also a column in Google Ads that helps you decide how high to bid.
If you use a paid advertising agency (a company that runs ads for you), **give them this number** as the target for optimizing your campaigns.
** The goal of bidding by product is to set the allowed ad spend per sale based on gross profit (money left after product cost). For example, spend up to **50%** of gross profit to get one sale.**
**Higher-priced products with the same margin can therefore justify higher bids.**
** Some competitive niches (crowded product markets) need about **$150 to $250** to start a Google Product Listing Ad campaign.**
**A Product Listing Ad is a Google ad that shows your product's picture and price. Budget for this before launching in a crowded category.**
**ROAS (return on ad spend) = revenue from ads / ad spend.** A target of 10x means 100 dollars of ad spend should return 1,000
dollars in revenue.
Maximum acceptable ad cost per order = average order value (AOV, the average amount one customer spends per order) **divided by target ROAS**.
Example: an average order value of 1,000 dollars at a 10x ROAS allows up to 100 dollars of ad cost per sale.
** For a strong Google Shopping campaign, target at least **10x** return on ad spend within two to five days of the click.
ROAS formula and the 10x benchmark (continued)
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Target ROAS of **10x**: every 1 dollar of ad spend should return at least 10 dollars in sales. This target applies after the first two to three weeks of the campaign learning phase (the time Google needs to learn), not on day one.
** Minimum ROAS threshold: maintain at least **10x** return on ad spend to achieve profitability. Scale upward gradually (increase spend slowly) while keeping ROAS above 10x.
** Keep at least **10:1 ROAS**, meaning 10 USD back for each dollar spent, while raising the budget. Increase spend for as long as the ratio holds.
For Google Shopping, the baseline target is a **blended ROAS of at least 10x** across all campaigns. Blended means one average for all campaigns together.
Products priced too low for their cost per sale fall below this target and need optimizing (improving) first.
** The ROAS target for Google Shopping is at least **10x**. If an agency runs category campaigns instead of Alpha and Beta, judge them only by ROAS against this minimum.**
**Alpha and Beta are two Google Shopping campaigns, explained below.**
The 10x ROAS target and the ad-cost rule of thumb (ad cost per sale equals one tenth of the order value) were given specifically for Google Ads.

Treat them as a Google Ads benchmark (a reference standard), **not a universal target** for all ad platforms.
(2023) The minimum target ROAS stayed at **10X**.
** Goal is **10x** return on ad spend, which should be reachable within a few weeks with minor campaign optimization.
** Maximum ad spend per sale = **10 percent** of the sale price. Example: a $1,500 sofa allows up to $150 of ad cost to earn one sale.
** At a cost per click (CPC) of $1, a $150 budget buys 150 clicks. If those clicks produce 2 sales, the ad cost per sale is **$75**. If only one sale results, the cost per sale doubles.
** Conversion rates (the share of visitors who buy) and click costs vary by product. Use the 10 percent ceiling as a starting point, and adjust bids with real campaign data.
Campaign-Level ROAS targets
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Target ROAS for the Alpha campaign is around **15X** (about $15 revenue per $1 of ad spend).
For the Beta campaign it is around **8X** ($8 per $1). Alpha bids are set higher because its keywords convert better.
The ROAS figures for the two Shopping campaigns (about 15X for the high-converting Alpha campaign and about 8X for the broader Beta campaign) are planning benchmarks.
They show how much revenue each dollar of ad spend should bring back. They justify setting different bids per campaign.
They are **not entered as a target** in a Manual CPC setup, where you set each click price yourself.
** Google Shopping with about **5x** ROAS should receive most of the budget.**
**Facebook retargeting (showing ads to past visitors) below 1x ROAS should be **cut or stopped**, since it overspends on people who are already reachable.**
(2020 example) For the 15x example in the scaling procedure, see **Scaling Rules**.
Source conflict: Source C (an e-commerce mentoring program) gives a **3x to 4x** target ROAS for a Google Shopping start with a $500 to $1,500 starting budget.
The Source A sources above set **10x** as the minimum for Google Shopping. Both values are given here because they come from different sources and setups.
**Use 10x** as the profitability floor (the lowest level that still makes profit). Check which setup you are running before applying 3x to 4x.
Set maximum PPC ad spend (pay-per-click, where you pay for each click) at **no more than 10 percent** of total monthly
revenue. Example: $25,000 monthly revenue allows a maximum of $2,500 PPC spend. $2,500 monthly revenue allows a maximum of $250 PPC spend.

** Cap ad spend at **10%** of MAP per sale. MAP (minimum advertised price) is the lowest price a brand lets sellers advertise. For a $1,000 MAP product, the ad budget per sale should not exceed about $100.
(2023) A sales budget of **300 dollars per day** for about 1,100 sessions (visits to your site) was given as a high but acceptable amount of clicks, if they convert.

With an average order value of $1,000, you could spend up to about $100 in ads to get one sale. Even so, **start with a $5 to $30 daily budget** and let Google learn, rather than spending $100 per day.

** Use a **90/10 budget split**: 90% of the ad budget goes to Google Shopping (alpha beta) and 10% to remarketing (ads to past visitors). Google Shopping typically performs better on new traffic than other channels.
Price thresholds ($200 minimum)
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Products priced under **$200** are generally not worth running Google Shopping ads for,
because reaching a 10x ROAS on them is very difficult. Use $200 as the minimum price for products that receive ad spend. Products near $197 are borderline.

Lower-priced products are hard to make profitable under a 10x ROAS target, because ad cost per sale must stay low. Shops that want paid traffic should **avoid sales prices** far below a few hundred dollars.

Before setting up Shopping ads, **list every product** in the store priced above $200. Check which ones are not yet selling. Products already above the threshold are the first candidates for ad spend.
**Excluding unprofitable products** from Shopping campaigns also reduces negative keyword work. A negative keyword is a search word that blocks your ad.
An excluded product cannot be triggered by a search term and cannot spend money. Fixing the product set first removes a source of wasted spend before search terms need review.
Starting a new Google Shopping campaign at a low daily budget, such as **$10 per day**, is acceptable.
Low monthly spend alone should not be read as failure, because the cause may be bids or product prices rather than the budget.
Products without a **2X wholesale margin** get organic traffic only. Organic traffic means free visitors, not paid ads.

Wholesale is the price you pay your supplier. A 2X wholesale margin means the sale price is at least double the wholesale price. Ads should focus on products where wholesale is at most half the sale price.
Run ads only for products where the margin can cover ad spend. **Do not advertise** low-margin products. Negotiate better prices or drop those products. **
Advertise every product where your margin supports the cost of ads. **Remove** products from suppliers that do not enforce MAP (make sellers keep the minimum price). They will not perform. **
Products with a small margin should be **excluded** from paid campaigns when ad spend would be unprofitable. High-margin products keep their paid campaigns.
Do not spend ad budget on products where competitors sell at unprofitable prices, below your **2x wholesale** minimum. Example: with a $500 wholesale cost, your minimum price is $1,000.
If competitors sell at $800 (20% below your $1,000 price), your ads would likely not convert against those cheaper offers. Convert means turning a visitor into a buyer.
**Check** Google Shopping listings to see what competitors charge for the same product.
Compare those prices with your 2x wholesale minimum before setting your sale price or deciding whether to run paid ads.
What to do with products you cannot sell profitably against competitors
1. List the product on your store at your **full minimum price of 2x wholesale**.
2. Let it be found through **free traffic** sources rather than paid ads.
3. **Do not run paid ads** for it while it appears next to competitors selling at unprofitable prices.
Run Google Ads **only on products from suppliers that actively enforce MAP** policies.
MAP (minimum advertised price) is the lowest price a brand allows sellers to advertise. Enforcing means the brand checks and stops sellers who go below it.
Do not allocate ad spend to products from suppliers without MAP enforcement. Competitors will price below your cost and remove your profit.
Products whose sellers price below the brand's MAP, which removes your margin, should be excluded from Google Shopping campaigns.
Suppliers do not all enforce MAP, so **check enforcement** before advertising a product.
For products with MAP restrictions, **use asterisks and exclusions** on the /promotions page to list brands that cannot be discounted. An exclusion means leaving an item out of the sale.
This satisfies supplier agreements while still running promotions to your full warm audience (people who already know your shop).

If a MAP-compliant supplier also sells on marketplaces such as eBay, Amazon, or Walmart at MAP, you may list them on your site. **Do not pay for ads** to them. Rely only on organic traffic for those sales. **
At **2.5%** conversion, two and a half sales come from every 100 targeted visitors.
A quality-traffic goal of **2.5%** from Google Shopping means at 300 clicks you should expect at least 6 to 7 sales, possibly up to 10.
** About **100 unique clicks** (clicks from different people) should produce around 2 sales within about 3 days at the 2.5% goal.
Increase the Google Ads budget until the store gets about **100 targeted clicks per week**, which should lead to roughly 2 to 3 sales. Count clicks across all campaigns combined. **
** Traffic check: if this produces about **75 unique clicks per day** at $1 CPC, with the 2.5% target conversion rate, the store can generate consistent revenue.
** Traffic consistency check: for a store to run consistently, roughly **75 qualified unique clicks per day** at about 2.5% conversion is enough traffic in the beginning.**
**Combine this with remarketing to win back visitors who did not buy.**
Budget to clicks and sales
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: A daily Google Ads budget is roughly the monthly budget **divided by 30**. **

At $1 cost per click, a **$33 daily budget** buys about 100 clicks every three days. If the conversion rate is 2%, that produces about two sales in that period. That gives enough data to decide on scaling. **

With a $33 daily Google Ads budget, $1 cost per click, and a store that converts at 2%, a first sale is expected within about **three days** after the store, supplier approvals and products are set up. **
With $1,000 per month, $1 average cost per click, and a 1% conversion rate target, expect about **one conversion every three days**.
This frequency provides enough data points to test and optimize before scaling spend.
At $1 CPC and a 1% conversion rate with a $33 daily budget, you get roughly **one conversion every three days** (100 clicks over three days).
With a broad Google campaign (one that reaches many searches), a cost per click under **$1** is realistic. For example, a $180 budget might produce about 200 clicks. **
** A **$3 cost per click** is probably too high for most niches. Only a broad, very competitive keyword with huge search volume (many people searching it) could justify a bid that high.
Adjust the starting budget to the cost per click. With a $2 CPC, the budget may be raised to about **$60 per day**.
With a $0.50 CPC, it could be cut to about half of $33, or kept at $33 to get more clicks and conversions sooner.

Sales should appear within **1 to 3 days** of a click if ads are optimized.
(2020) Sales should show within **a few days** if the campaign is set up correctly.
** A first sale is expected within about **three days** after the store, supplier approvals and products are set up.
** A starting Google Ads budget of about **$1,000 per month** covers the entire product catalog (all your products together), not each product separately.
Learning-Speed Math
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: A lower daily budget takes proportionally longer to gather enough click and sales data for optimization decisions.
A $5 per day budget needs **six times as long** as $30 per day to produce the same data (30 divided by 5 is 6).
A budget of 15 dollars per day roughly **doubles** the time needed to collect enough data for decisions, compared with $30 per day.
Target conversion rate for Google Ads campaigns is **2.5 percent**.
Use this as a benchmark (a reference point) to check whether campaign performance is on track.
Target conversion rate from Google Shopping ads is **2.5%**, meaning two and a half sales per 100 targeted visitors. **
Google Ads conversion goal for the store is a **2.5% conversion rate**. About 100 unique clicks should produce around 2 sales within about 3 days. **
A typical e-commerce site (online shop) running Google Ads should expect a conversion rate of roughly **1% to 2%**.

A store with a lower rate, such as 0.5%, can still be profitable if its lifetime value (total money one customer spends over time) or cart value is higher. The acceptable rate depends on the business economics.
As a rough benchmark, the buy-ready segment at the bottom of the funnel (people ready to buy) converts at about **1% to 3%**. Check this figure against your own account data before planning budgets.

Conversion-rate planning figures in the sources differ: **1%** (target for a $1,000 monthly start), **2%** (example store), and **2.5%** (Google Shopping goal). Use the figure that matches your own account data.

Treat 2.5% as the goal and 1% to 2% as the typical range.
Traffic at a 2.5% target conversion rate should be checked against your own data before budgets are set.

p.t: Minimum Google Ads budget is **5 dollars per day**, and a typical starting budget is 30 dollars per day.
Anything between 5 and 30 dollars per day is a reasonable test budget for a first campaign.
Start Google Ads with a daily budget **between $5 and $30**. Give Google about 2 to 4 weeks to learn before judging performance.
Start Google Shopping campaigns with a budget of **5 to 30 dollars a day**, which is enough to gather data and decide how to scale. **
For a brand-new store, a combined daily budget of **$5 to $30** across the two Google Shopping campaigns (Alpha and Beta) is the workable range. Combined means one total for both.
$30 per day gives data fastest. (2023)
Starting daily budget: **$5 to $10 per day** is recommended for most people. The maximum the author goes to for a new store and new Ads account is $30 per day.

Starting small lets Google learn before scaling profitable campaigns.
Initial Google Ads budget for new stores: **$10 to $30 per day**. **

Starting daily ad budget: **$10 to $30 per day**. (2023)
A starting ad budget of **$10 to $30 per day** is enough. Use Google Ads vouchers, which give free credit to start. **
Starting daily Google Ads budget: **10 to 30 dollars per day**, spent on optimizing the traffic rather than waiting for sales. (2023)
Starting Google Ads budget: **10 to 30 USD per day**. Many stores start at about 30 USD per day, and 10 USD per day is the lowest practical starting level. **
New stores typically start Google Ads with **10 to 30 dollars per day** and scale over time. A 10 dollar daily test budget is a common starting point for testing. **

p.t: A new Google Ads account must eventually be cross-checked (double-checked against a second source).
All new Google Shopping products start with a daily budget **between 10 and 30 dollars per day**. The maximum recommended is 30 dollars per day and the minimum 10 dollars per day.

A lower budget gives slower data. (2024)
Typical starting budgets are **$10 to $30 per day**, not the full monthly allocation. (2024)
A new store can start with about **$30 per day** in ad budget and scale up profitably. Budgets are increased only when ROAS holds. **
Start with a daily budget of **20 to 30 USD** and scale up the campaigns that are profitable while cutting the ones that are not. **
Start Google Shopping with a daily budget of **20 to 30 USD**. The usual starting range is 20 to 30 USD per day when the budget allows. **
Start Google Shopping at **$20 to $30 per day**. This allows enough daily data to make informed optimizations every 2 weeks without overspending. **
Plan for a minimum of **USD 20 per day** in marketing spend when starting, mainly on Google Ads through the Google Search Network (Google's search results and partner sites).
Spending less is possible but not recommended.
Start paid traffic for a newly launched product at a small daily budget, around **10 USD per day**.
Increase spend only on products that prove profitable, with a strong MAP-to-wholesale spread (a big gap between the MAP price and the wholesale price) and good conversion. (2025)
Launch Google Shopping with a small test budget of about **$10 per day** and keep it unchanged until it is profitable. The account then collects data on which products get clicks and sales. (2025)
With two verified suppliers and about 50 products, small test budgets can be run to get the products approved and see traffic, while sourcing (finding products to buy) continues in the background. **
Maximum starting budgets
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: A maximum starting daily budget of about **$30** is suggested for Google campaigns, and smaller starts are acceptable. (2024)
For a new Google Shopping account, cap the daily budget at about **30 per day**. 50 per day is too high early on. **

In the 2021 Google Shopping setup described, a new account should start with a maximum shared daily budget of about **30 per day**. A shared budget is one daily money pot that several campaigns share.
50 per day is considered too high for a store with a small uploaded catalog. The catalog should first be expanded so Google has more products to optimize across.
Start Google Shopping with a **$30 per day** budget, with the option to start at $10 per day when money is tight.
Budgets for Google Shopping and Meta remarketing together came to about $30 to $35 per day in 2023. Meta is the company behind Facebook and Instagram ads. The minimum target ROAS stayed at 10X.
Do not set a Google Ads daily budget far below **$10 per day**, because campaigns need enough budget to spend and collect data.
The usual starting point is about $30 per day, and $10 per day is the lowest reasonable start. (2023)
**Ignore** Google's suggested budget increases, such as a recommended $90 per day, because those suggestions aim to increase your spend. Set budgets based on your own sales data. (2026)
Starting daily ad budget = $15 (bestseller shared budget for Google alpha and beta) + $5 (everything-else shared budget for Google alpha
and beta) + $5 (Meta remarketing) = **$25 per day**. A bestseller is one of your best-selling products. Microsoft and Bing are excluded from the starting budget. (2024)
Beginner launch sequence (2019 example)

p.t: Starting budget of **$200** consists of the $100 credit plus $100 of the store owner's own money.

The 2019 credit for new Shopify stores (Shopify is the software that runs online shops) was $100.
**Google Shopping (product listing ads)**

Budget: $180
Setting: $20 per day, running about 9 days
**Facebook remarketing (dynamic product ads)**

Budget: $20
Setting: $5 per day, retargeting visitors who came from Google

Dynamic product ads show each visitor the exact product they looked at. The 2019 example estimated total spend at about $215. The budget is spread over several days so Google has time to collect data. **
1. **Finish setting up and optimizing the store** before spending on ads.
2. Set the Google Shopping daily budget to **$20** instead of $30 to $50, so the budget lasts about nine days.
3. **Do not spend the whole budget on day one**; allow several days of data.
4. Set a Facebook remarketing campaign with a simple dynamic product ad group at **$5 per day**, retargeting people who came from Google.
5. Start the **daily audit** process (a daily check of your numbers) from day one.
1. Start a Google Shopping campaign.
2. Set a daily budget of **$25 to $50** when working with a starting budget of $500 to $1,500.

3. Set a target ROAS of **3x to 4x**, for example aiming for $200 in sales from $50 of spend.
4. Let the products appear in Shopping. No extra campaign structure is needed at the start.

Monthly caps and test budgets
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: A starting Google Ads budget of about $1,000 per month is typical. This equals approximately $33 per day.
A recommended starting budget for a new Shopping (PPC) account is at least $1,000 per month, which equals $33 per day.
A first Google Ads budget of about $500 to $1,000 per month is reasonable. Sales should show within a few days if the campaign is set up correctly.
A new store can start with about $500 to $1,000 per month in ads, which works out to roughly $15 to $35 per day. Spending above that level should come from reinvested store profit.
A $1,000 first month is based on a $30 per day Google Shopping budget. Starting at $10 per day is fine but gives slower data. (2023)
A first month test budget of about 1,000 dollars can be spent as 30 dollars per day on Google Shopping shared between alpha and beta, 3 to 5 dollars per day on Google remarketing
and 3 to 5 dollars per day on Facebook remarketing, then scaled once conversions appear.
With a $3,000 monthly budget, $2,700 goes to Google Shopping.
The remaining $300 goes to remarketing, split into $200 per month for Facebook dynamic product ads and $100 per month for Google remarketing.
With a total ad budget of 100 USD, put about 90 USD into Google Ads and about 10 USD into Facebook dynamic remarketing.
Budget split between channels: about 90% of advertising budget goes to Google Ads, and about 10% goes to Facebook remarketing to bring people back to the store.
Alpha and Beta test split (2019 example): Alpha campaign (high-priority, high-bid, converting keywords) set to $30 daily budget.
Beta campaign (high-priority, low-bid, weak keywords) set to $17 daily budget.
A $25 Google budget can be split so that each of the alpha and beta campaigns gets $12.50. (2024)
Daily Google Ads budget is roughly the monthly budget divided by 30. A starting budget of $1,000 per month equals about $33 per day.
Adjust the starting budget to the cost per click; see the cost-per-click rule under Expected Clicks and Conversions.
Scaling Rules
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: Start Google Ads with small budgets and optimize every two weeks.
Starting with large budgets and letting campaigns run without tweaks is what causes thousands of dollars to be spent with zero conversions. (2024)
Start Google Shopping campaigns with small initial budgets. Scale spending upward only as performance data proves profitability.
Buy data first: the starting budget is for collecting data on which products get clicks and sales, not for scaling.
** Starting with a small budget is for collecting data: impressions, clicks and purchases show which products people find and buy.**
**Use that data to add negatives and adjust cost per click per product, then increase budget once return on ad spend improves a few days after optimizing.**
Scale the budget gradually with ROAS above 10x, and only as profitable campaigns prove the ratio.
Products with a strong MAP-to-wholesale spread and good conversion are the only ones that should receive increased spend.

The scaling procedure for Google Ads budgets is:
1. Set a target ROAS for the current budget, for example 15x on $2,000 spend.

2. Improve efficiency until that target holds.
3. Only then scale the budget, expecting ROAS to fall somewhat as spend grows.
Increase the budget as long as ROAS holds; the ratio is the signal to raise spend.
Add money in steps: after the first 2 to 4 weeks of learning, judge the campaign on the data and do not scale on day one.
The learning phase for the ROAS target is the first two to three weeks of a campaign.
Use the 2019 approach: scale up the campaigns that are profitable while cutting the ones that are not.
Keep the test budget unchanged until it is profitable, apply the Google Ads optimizations, and only then scale the budget by reinvesting profits from existing sales. (2025)
Scale spending for a product only after it proves profitable and reinvest store profits into ads once the free credits are used.
The budget for the second half of the first month is raised only after conversions appear, not before.
Budget can increase with a profitable ROAS, with no upward limit set in the 2023 source.
Ad credits and promotional vouchers
p.s: Unit economics before spending: break-even, target ROAS and budget

p.t: **Credit and voucher offers**
Google Ads and Microsoft Ads offer discount codes for new advertiser accounts. When first setting up advertising, ask about or search for promotional codes to reduce your initial ad spend. (2024)
Use Google Ads vouchers, which provide free credit to start.
When creating a Google Ads account, select Offer A to spend $500 and receive a $500 credit. No money is lost if spending does not reach $500.
Google Ads promotional offers come as coupon codes, either a fixed dollar credit or a matching offer. Matching offers change over time, so check the current terms before signing up.
A current matching offer in the US pays back spend up to $150, but only if the spend happens within the first 30 days after the Google Ads account is created.
Verify the exact amount and window in the offer terms shown at the bottom of the coupon page.
The matching offer window of 30 days starts when the Google Ads account is created, not when the coupon code is received. Create the account only when the spend for the next 30 days is ready.
Google's sign-up promotion for new Google Ads accounts (as shown in 2020s lessons, may change): spend $500 within the first 60 days to receive $500 in free advertising credit.
Higher tiers of $1,000 and $1,500 spend are unrealistic for a beginner budget, so the lowest tier is the sensible choice.
The 2024 offers are: a Google Ads credit of $1,000 after $1,500 in ad spend, and a Microsoft Ads credit of $500 after $500 in spend, with both requiring spending by November 30.
The Google Ads credit offer ($500 credit for $500 spend in 60 days) and the Bing offer ($500 credit for $250 spend) together can add up to $750 in free ad credit.
Ad credits and promotional vouchers (continued)

p.t: This justifies spending at least the required amount during the launch window. (2024)
Source conflict on the Microsoft or Bing credit: one 2024 source gives $500 after $500 in spend, and another gives $500 after $250 in spend. Use the terms shown in the offer itself.

Source conflict on the Google credit window: the same $500 for $500 offer is described with a 60-day window (, ), while the matching offer described in has a 30-day window. Check which offer type is shown.
** Google, Bing and Facebook ad credits offered at signup were worth about $200 to $300 in total for a new store. These are 2020 offers, so check current offers before relying on them.
** After the free ad credits are used, set aside a couple hundred dollars for ads and then reinvest store profits into ads.
A bonus gift can lower advertising cost, not only raise sales.
When the bonus removes the reason to compare prices, buyers purchase on their first visit instead of leaving, searching again and clicking a paid ad a second time, so the cost per sale falls.
You pay for every click in Google Ads, including clicks from visitors who never buy. Irrelevant or poorly matched traffic therefore costs money with no sales in return.
Irrelevant and wasted spend is reduced by excluding unprofitable products and by adding negatives after data is collected.
In Google Ads, the ad for a niche with a higher ad spend should show roughly 1,100 sessions for about 300 dollars per day;
the question to ask is whether the traffic converts into sales, not just whether the clicks are high.
